title: Devender Dutt Sharma vs Usha Sharma on 18 March, 2015
full_text: Devender Dutt Sharma vs Usha Sharma on 18 March, 2015 IN THE COURT OF SHRI SUNIL GUPTA, M.M (NE) KARKARDOOMA COURTS, DELHI CC No. : 32/13 U/s : 138 N. I. Act Devender Dutt Sharma Vs Usha Sharma Unique Case ID No. 02402R0125062006 J U D G E M E N T 1. Sl. No. of the case : 32/2013 ( RBT ) 2. Date of institution of the case : 24.05.2008 3. Name of complainant : Sh. Ravi Sharma s/o Late Sh. B.D. Sharma r/o H.No. 5/236, A­Lalita Park, Laxmi Nagar, Delhi ( substituted on 30.10.2009 in place Mr. Devender Dutt Sharma who expired during trial) 4. Date of commission of offence : 28.01.2006 5. Name of accused, parentage & address : Usha Sharma s/o Late Sh. K.K. Mohan, r/o 56, Naishvilla Road (GF), Dehradoon, Uttaranchal. 6. Offence complained of or proved : 138 N. I. Act 7. Plea of accused : Accused pleaded not guilty 8. Final order : Convicted 9. Date of which order was reserved : 26.02.2015 10.Date of pronouncement : 18.03.2015 BRIEF REASONS FOR THE DECISION OF THE CASE 1. It is stated by the complainant in his complaint that in the month of September 2005, accused Usha Sharma approached him to take a loan of Rs.1,50,000/­ to discharge her financial liabilities. As complainant was CC No. 32/13(RBT). 1 of 15 having good faith upon the accused who was his bhabhi ( wife of his younger brother ), so the complainant has given Rs. 1,50,000/­ to the accused as friendly loan. Complainant asked accused to execute a promissory note, receipt, affidavit and agreement, and also asked her to issue him post­dated cheques of the loan amount. It is further alleged that respondent agreed all the terms and conditions as offered by the complainant and issued two post­dated cheques for an amount of Rs. 1,05,000/­ and Rs. 45,000/­ apart from issuing a separate receipt of receiving the loan amount. Accused also signed and thumbed a promissory note. Both parties has also executed an affidavit and an agreement duly notarized at New Delhi and attested in the presence of the accused and witnesses. It is further alleged that complainant contacted the accused at Dehradoon in the second week of January 2006 to recover/return his loan amount as he was in need of money on which accused asked him that he can withdraw amount of Rs. 45,000/­ from the cheuqe and after 4­5 days, the other cheque can also be presented for encashment. It is alleged that when complainant presented the cheque of Rs.1,05,000/­ on 18.01.2006, the same was dishonored on account of "insufficient funds". When complainant asked accused about dishonor of aforesaid cheque, she could not give any satisfactory reply and tried to avoid making payment. Thereafter complainant served a legal demand notice dated 07.02.2006 to the accused by registered AD and UPC asking her to make the payment CC No. 32/13(RBT). 2 of 15 within stipulated period. The said payment not having been made, the present case was filed under Section 138 Negotiable Instrument Act was filed. 2. On the basis of pre­summoning evidence, accused was summoned for the offence under Section 138 Negotiable Instrument Act on 03.03.2006 by Ld. Predecessor Court. Accused put her appearance on 25.04.2006, and thereafter a notice under Section 251 Cr.P.C was framed against the accused on 16.05.2007 by Ld. Predecessor Court, to which she pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. 3. During the course of trial, the complainant Mr. Devender Dutt Sharma expired and his son Mr. Ravi Sharma was substituted vide order dated 30.10.2009 of Ld. Predecessor. The substituted complainant Mr. Ravi Sharma was examined as CW­1. Smt. Karuna Sharma ( aunt of CW1 ) was examined as CW2. Thereafter, complainant's evidence was closed. The complainant has relied upon the documents i.e Ex. CW1/A1 to CW1/A5, Ex.B1 to B4, Ex. C1, Ex. C2, & Ex. D. Mr. Ravi Sharma, and Smt. Karuna Sharma has been cross­examined at length by Ld. Defence Counsel. 4. After conclusion of complainant's post summoning evidence, statement of accused was recorded under Section 313 Cr.P.C on 28.05.2012 wherein accused submitted that she came to know about the withdrawal of amount of Rs. 45,000/­ from her account on 18.01.2006 and she instructed her banker to stop payment against the other stolen cheque. She has also lodged CC No. 32/13(RBT). 3 of 15 an FIR in respect of stolen cheque with P.S Kotwali, Dehradoon. She has examined two witnesses from Punjab National Bank, Paltan Bazar Branch, Dehradoon, Uttarakhand in her defence. 5. I have carefully gone through the record and heard the arguments on behalf of both the parties. 6. Now Section 138 Negotiable Instrument Act provides as under :­ Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in the account- Where any cheque drawn by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker for payment of any amount of money to another person from out of that account for the discharge, in whole or in part, or any debt or other liability, is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement made with that bank, such person shall be deemed to have committed an offence and shall, without prejudice to any other provisions of this Act, be punished with imprisonment for [ a term which may be extended to two years], or with fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque, or with both: Provided that nothing contained in this Section shall apply unless­­ i) that cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier; ii) the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, as the case CC No. 32/13(RBT). 4 of 15 may be, makes a demand for the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice in writing, to the drawer of the cheque, [within thirty days] of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid; and iii) the drawer of such cheque fails to make payment of the said amount of money to the payee or, as the case may be, to the holder in due course of the cheque, within fifteen days of the receipt of the said notice. So the perusal of the Section shows that complainant has to prove following things in order to prove his case :­ i) the cheque was drawn by the accused for payment of due amount to the complainant; ii) the amount was due on the part of the accused for discharge of any legally enforceable debt or other liability; iii) the cheque was returned dishonoured; iv) the legal notice was given to the accused within stipulated period; v) even after the receipt of the legal notice, the accused chose not to make the payment. Ld. Counsel for the complainant has submitted that the complainant has satisfied and proved all the ingredients of the offence under Section 138 Negotiable Instrument Act. He has further submitted that presumptions under Section 118 & 139 Negotiable Instrument Act are also there and in view of the aforesaid presumptions, the case of the complainant has been proved. The presumptions mentioned above are as under :­ Section 118 Negotiable Instrument Act­ Presumption as to negotiable instruments. Until the contrary is proved, the following presumptions shall CC No. 32/13(RBT). 5 of 15 be made :­ a) of consideration­­ that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration, and that every such instrument, when it has been accepted, endorsed, negotiated or transferred, was accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration; b) as to date­­ that every negotiable instrument bearing a date was made or drawn on such date; c) as to time of acceptance--that every accepted bill of exhange was accepted within a reasonable time after its date and before its maturity;.......... Section 139 Negotiable Instrument Act­ Presumption in favor of holder.­­ It shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque of the nature referred to in Section 138 for the discharge, in whole or in part, or any debt or other liability. 7. It has been submitted by Ld Counsel for the complainant that as the complainant has successfully proved his case so the accused be convicted for the offence under Section 138 N.I. Act whereas Ld. Defence Counsel has submitted that no case is made out against the accused. Ld. Defence Counsel has submitted that the legal notice in question sent to the accused was allegedly delivered by the postal authorities on 16.02.2006. It has also been submitted that the present CC No. 32/13(RBT). 6 of 15 case has been filed before the Court on 01.03.2006 and in view of the recent judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in case titled as Yogender Pratap Singh vs. Savitri Pandey & Anr. Dated 19.09.2014, the present complaint case is pre­mature and hence no case is made out against the accused. Even otherwise, it has been submitted that the cheque in question was stolen by the complainant Mr. Devender Dutt ( since expired) and there was no liability of the accused towards him. I have heard the submissions from both the sides. In view of the Court, it will be appropriate if the question as to whether the present complaint case was filed pre­mature is dealt with first, in view of the judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in case titled as Yogender Pratap Singh ( supra). This question is vital because if the answer is in affirmative then no purpose shall be served by examining other material on record. As per the complainant, the legal notice dated 07.01.2006 ( wrongly dated as 07.01.2006, it should have been 07.02.2006 as per the complainant) was sent to the accused on 07.02.2006 through registered A/D. The letter was not delivered to the accused and same was accordingly returned with the remarks " unclaimed returned to sender". The CC No. 32/13(RBT). 7 of 15 envelope in question is on record. On the front side of the envelope there are three stamps to the effect " unclaimed returned to sender". On its back side, first endorsement is not clear but thereafter signatures are there with the date 11/2. Immediately thereafter, there is another date mentioned as 14/2. After that endorsement to the effect N/D is there and there are signatures with the date 15/2. Then there is another date 16/2 after this. The argument of the defence is that if statutory period of 15 days as provided under Negotiable Instrument Act, 1881 is counted from 16.02.2006 then the present complaint case is pre­mature considering the fact that February 2006 was having only 28 days. It has also been argued by defence that no other interpretation is permissible in the aforementioned facts. On the other hand, Ld Counsel for the complainant has submitted that the attempt has been made by the postman to deliver the letter/legal notice on 11.02.2006 also and for that reason, the matter is not premature. After going through the record, it is not disputed that the legal notice in question was not received by the accused. Had the legal notice been received by the accused against her signatures then there would not have been any controversy regarding the date from which CC No. 32/13(RBT). 8 of 15 the period of limitation is to be counted. The observations of Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in a case titled as K.Bhaskaran vs. Sankaran Vaidhyan Balan & Anr. dated 29.09.1999 are worth mentioning in this context : The more important point to be decided in this case is whether the cause of action has arisen at all as the notice sent by the complainant to the accused was returned as `unclaimed.' The conditions pertaining to the notice to be given to the drawer, have been formulated and in­ corporated in clauses (b) and (c) of the proviso to Section 138(1) of the Act. The said clauses are extracted below : "(b) The payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, as the case may be, makes a demand for the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice in writing, to the drawer of the cheque, within fif­ teen days of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid; and (c) the drawer of such cheque fails to make the payment of the said amount of money to the payee or as the case may be, to the holder in due course of the cheque within fifteen days of the receipt of the said notice." On the part of the payee he has to make a demand by `giving a notice' in writing. If that was the only requirement to complete the offence on the failure of the drawer to pay the cheque amount within 15 days from the date of such `giving' the travails of the prosecution would have been very much lessened. But the legislature says that failure on the part of the drawer to pay the amount should be within 15 days `of the receipt' of the said notice. It is, therefore, clear that `giving notice' in the context is not the same as receipt of notice. Giving is a process of which receipt is the accomplishment. It is for the payee to perform CC No. 32/13(RBT). 9 of 15 the former process by sending the notice to the drawer in the correct address. In Black's Law Dictionary, `giving of notice' is distinguished from `re­ ceiving of the notice.' (vide page 621) "A person notifies or gives no­ tice to another by taking such steps as may be reasonably required to inform the other in the ordinary course, whether or not such other ac­ tually comes to know of it." A person `receives' a notice when it is duly delivered to him or at the place of his business. If a strict interpretation is given that the drawer should have actually received the notice for the period of 15 days to start running no mat­ ter that the payee sent the notice on the correct address, a trickster cheque drawer would get the premium to avoid receiving the notice by different strategies and he could escape­from the legal consequences of Section 138 of the Act. It must be borne in mind that Court should not adopt in interpretation which helps a dishonest evader and clips an honest payee as that would defeat the very legislative measure. In Maxwell's `Interpretation of Statues' the learned author has em­ phasized that "provisions relating to giving of notice often receive lib­ eral interpretation." (vide page 99 of the 12th edn.) The context envis­ aged in Section 138 of the Act invites a liberal interpretation for the person who has the statutory obligation to give notice because he is presumed to be the loser in the transaction and it is for his interest the very provision is made by the legislature. The words in clause (b) of the proviso to Section 138 of the Act show that payee has the statutory obligation to `make a demand' by giving notice. The thrust in the clause is on the need to `make a­demand'. It is only the mode for mak­ ing such demand which the legislature has prescribed. A payee can send the notice for doing his part for giving the notice. Once it is despatched his part is over and the next depends on what the sendee does. CC No. 32/13(RBT). 10 of 15 It is well settled that a notice refused to be accepted by the addressee can be presumed to have been served on him, [vide Harcharan Singh v. Smt. Shivrani and Ors. , [1981] 2 SCC 535, and Jagdish Singh v. Natthu Singh , [1992] 1 SCC 647.] Here the notice is returned as un­ claimed and not as refused. Will there be any significant different be­ tween the two so far as the presumption of service is concerned? In this connection a reference to Section 27 of the General Clauses Act will be useful. The Section reads thus : "27. Meaning of service by post. ­ Where any central Act or Regula­ tion made after the commencement of this Act authorizes or requires any document to be served by post, whether the expression `serve' or either of the expressions `give' or `send' or any other expression is used, then, unless a different intention appears, the service shall be deemed to be effected by properly addressing, pre­paying and posting by registered post, a letter containing the document, and unless the contrary is proved, to have been effected at the time at which the let­ ter would be delivered in the ordinary course of post" No doubt Section 138 of the Act does not require that the notice should be given only by `post'. Nonetheless the principle incorporated in Section 27 (quoted above) can profitably be imported in a case where the sender has despatched the notice by post with the correct address written on it. Then it can be deemed to have been served on the sendee unless he proves that it was not really served and that he was not responsible for such non­service. Any other interpretation can lead to a very tenuous position as the drawer of the cheque who is liable to pay the amount would resort to the strategy of subterfuge by successfully avoiding the notice. Thus, when a notice is returned by the sendee as unclaimed such date would be the commencing date in reckoning the period of 15 days contemplated in clause (c) to the proviso of Section 138 of the Act. Of course such reckoning would be without prejudice to the right of the CC No. 32/13(RBT). 11 of 15 drawer of the cheque to show that he had no knowledge that the no­ tice was brought to his address. In the present case the accused did not even attempt to discharge the burden to rebut the aforesaid pre­ sumption" Reliance is also placed upon the judgment of Hon'ble Delhi High Court in Prakash Jewellers vs. A.K Jewellers dated 15.05.2002. It is true that the complainant has not led any evidence on the point of delivery of legal notice but it is also to be seen that he has alleged about the respondent having not received the registered A/D deliberately with the connivance of the postman. The substituted complainant Mr. Ravi Sharma has also stated to the same effect in his evidence by way of affidavit. He has not been cross­examined on this particular aspect by Ld. Defence Counsel despite there being lengthy cross­examination on other aspects. The accused on her part has merely denied, in her statement under Section 313 Cr.P.C, the receipt of the legal notice. She did not lead any evidence on her behalf on this particular aspect. She also did not state as to whether the officials from the postal department having visited her premises for this purpose, was within her knowledge or not. From the endorsements on the back side of the envelope on record, it is clear that the official concerned visited the premises of the accused on four CC No. 32/13(RBT). 12 of 15 different occasions i.e 11.02.2006, 14.02.2006, 15.02.2006 & 16.02.2006. The address on the envelope is not disputed nor the fact that the accused was residing at the relevant time at this address only. The only issue raised by Ld. Defence Counsel is that the date for counting the period of 15 days available to the accused for making the payment in this case is 16.02.2006. I am unable to see any justifiable ground for doing so. I am also unable to find any reason as to why the said period cannot be counted from 11.02.2006 itself. More so, when the address on the envelope is stated to be correct and no evidence at all has been led by the accused to rebut the presumption as explained by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in the case titled as K.Bhaskaran (supra). Simple denial by the accused qua the receipt of the legal notice is of no consequence at all. Accordingly, this Court holds that the present complaint case was not filed prematurely. As already mentioned, the emphasis of the defence was on getting declared the present complaint case as premature, hence detailed arguments were not adduced on merits. Even then, it is to be seen that the signatures on the cheque in question ( Ex. B1) are not denied by the accused. The returning memo ( Ex. B2) is also not in dispute. The discussion regarding the legal notice having been delivered on CC No. 32/13(RBT). 13 of 15 11.02.2006 has been narrated above. It is not in dispute that no payment was made by the accused even after that. Nothing material could be elicited by the defence from the two complainant witnesses. The signatures on the supporting documents i.e Agreement Ex. A1, Affidavit Ex. A2, Promissory Note Ex. A3 & Receipt Ex. A4 are also not denied. The accused has stated about these documents that the complainant ( the deceased ) on the pretext of getting her employed in place of her husband on compassionate ground made her sign on certain blank papers. Regarding the cheque in question, she has stated that same was stolen along with another cheque and she has lodged an FIR in respect of the same with P.S Kotwali. She has not examined any witnesses in her defence on this particular point. The two witnesses examined by her in her defence are officials of Punjab National Bank, Paltan Bazar branch, Dehradoon, Uttarakhand. The defence has failed to apprise this Court as to what material has come on record by examining these witnesses which could have been of any help to the accused. It is stated by the defence that the charge­sheet was filed against the complainant herein ( the late Mr. Devender Dutt Sharma ) but mere filing of the charge­sheet without there being any final judgment on the same by Ld. Court concerned cannot be of any CC No. 32/13(RBT). 14 of 15 significance. 8. Considering the above discussion, this Court is of the view that accused Usha Sharma has not been able to rebut the presumptions existing in favor of the complainant. Accordingly, accused Usha Sharma is held guilty and is convicted for the offence punishable u/s 138 of Negotiable Instrument Act. To come up for argument/order on sentence on 26.03.2015. Dictated & Announced in the open Court on 18.03.2015 ( SUNIL GUPTA ) METROPOLITAN MAGISTRATE(NE) KKD COURTS, SHAHDARA, DELHI CC No. 32/13(RBT). 15 of 15
